title: Grace (CCC 1996–2005)
hookLine: a free gift, God's own life shared with us

lines: PAY IT BACK? PAY IT FORWARD?
cards: Someone pays for your coffee in the drive-through line and drives off before you can thank them. What happens next varies.
Some people want to pay it back, or pay it forward right away, or explain why they didn't really need it. A gift that can't be repaid takes the account out of your hands.
Catholics say the life of God in the soul is exactly that kind of gift.

teach.b: Grace is the Latin gratia, and you can hear its cousin in gratis: free. The Greek is charis, a gift freely given.
Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." What is the gift?
The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives. Then it goes further.

teach.h: A SHARE IN GOD'S OWN LIFE.
teach.b: Grace is a share in God's own life. Not a thing God hands over from a distance: God giving himself. The Church names two kinds.
Sanctifying grace, today's word, is a lasting gift that makes a person holy and a friend of God, first given in baptism.
Actual graces are God's help in particular moments: the nudge to call someone, the strength to hold your tongue.

teach.h: THE TREE'S LIFE, THE DAY'S RAIN.
teach.b: One is like the life of a tree; the other, like the rain on a given day. And earning? Since the Reformation, Catholics and Protestants have argued about grace and merit, sometimes bitterly.

In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying together that people are accepted by God by grace alone, in faith in Christ, not because of any merit of their own.

teach.h: IT IS THE GIFT OF GOD.
teach.b: Catholics still speak of merit, and the Catechism explains that even merit is itself God's gift. A prayer of the Mass, drawing on Augustine, puts it this way: when God crowns our merits, he is crowning his own gifts.

how: Catholics believe sanctifying grace is first given in baptism and is restored and strengthened through the sacraments, especially confession and the Eucharist; some also pray for the actual graces they need for a particular day or task.

God's own life, given as a lasting gift

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the lasting gift, like a tree's life
help in a moment, like rain

s: in Catholic teaching, grace is a reward for being good enough
the Catechism calls grace free and undeserved: God's gift of his own life.
in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on grace

games.q: a stranger pays for your coffee and drives off before you can say anything. which response fits what today's teaching says about grace?
o: chase them down to pay them back.
simply receive it and say thank you.
buy coffee for the next car immediately.
games.why: simply receiving leaves the account in someone else's hands. Catholics say grace is exactly that kind of gift.

practice: Bring to mind something good in your life you did nothing to deserve: the family you were born into, a friend who stayed, your eyes, this morning's light.
Don't explain it or plan how to pay it back; just receive it, the way you'd open your hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Sanctifying grace. The lasting gift of God's own life, first given in baptism, that makes a person holy and a friend of God. Free, not earned.

orig.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. Latin gratia.

carryVoice: Your line: free, not earned. From the fall to the Word made flesh, Chalcedon, the Paschal mystery, the resurrection, the Spirit, and now grace: that was the week. Day three hundred eight, a full week.
